candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; administer blood and blood products safely, monitor transfusion therapy, and coordinate parenteral resuscitation
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — massive transfusion protocol in obstetric hemorrhage
candidate.educational_objective: Understand that an obstetric MTP enables rapid, coordinated multi-component blood-product resuscitation according to institutional protocol and evolving clinical/laboratory needs rather than requiring one universal component ratio.

options.A: The MTP supports rapid, coordinated delivery of red blood cells and other indicated blood components such as plasma and platelets according to the facility protocol while ongoing clinical and laboratory findings guide resuscitation.
options.B: Every obstetric MTP must use exactly the same 1:1:1 red-cell-to-plasma-to-platelet ratio because one universal ratio has been proven superior in obstetric hemorrhage.
options.C: An MTP provides crystalloid fluid only and is not intended to facilitate rapid blood-component support.
options.D: Massive transfusion protocols are limited to trauma care and should not be used for severe obstetric hemorrhage.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. AABB’s current massive-transfusion guidance supports organized protocols that enable transfusion services to provide blood components rapidly during massive hemorrhage. ACOG also recommends access to massive transfusion capability for severe obstetric hemorrhage and describes rapid replacement with red blood cells, plasma, and platelets while clinical and laboratory data guide care. Importantly, ACOG notes that controlled studies have not established one best blood-product ratio for obstetric hemorrhage, so B overstates the evidence. C and D misrepresent the purpose and obstetric applicability of MTPs.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Massive transfusion protocols provide organized rapid access to multiple blood components during severe hemorrhage, including obstetric hemorrhage; component ratios are protocol- and situation-dependent because one universally superior obstetric ratio has not been established.
